messages.subject: Bird surveys
parts:
Hi

I am just wondering whether Distance will be suitable for a particular study I am doing. I am looking at bird diversity and abundance on a farm that has a winter bird seed crop planted on it to aid bird conservation. I am looking at how birds use this crop into the winter. So I am doing weekly bird surveys which take into account what species were there and in what numbers. This is done in line with crop surveys to measure the dried weight of seeds per meter squared. So my question is, will distance allow me to enter data for more then one species at a time and will it let me do multiple weeks so that I can look at how the usage is changing throughout the winter. I would like to statistically test this and compare the different weeks etc etc. 

Many thanks

Jay

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Bird surveys
parts:
Jay:

The direct answer to your two questions are:

- can I enter data for more than a single species:  yes, create a field in the observation layer for species, then for each detection record the species
- can I 'do' multiple weeks: yes, you could think about treating weeks as strata

The Distance project "songbird" that is distributed with Distance as a sample project is likely closest to your situation.  That project has multiple species recorded (see "Species" field in Observation layer).  Data were gathered in 4 pastures across 2 years; consequently there are 8 strata, names 1980_x, where x is pasture number.  This example is in the Illustrative Examples Chapter of the Introduction to Distance Sampling Book, section 8.7. The data was gathered during an extensive survey of songbirds in the Arapaho National Wildlife Refuge in Colorado (Knopf et al. 1988).  The data are for two years and 4 pastures, and include multiple species.  Further details are in the Introduction to Distance Sampling book, or the original paper (Knopf et al. 1988. JWM 52:280-290).

You can produce stratum-specific estimates (by species, assuming sufficient numbers of sightings and transects) to make your statistical comparisons.  See Section 3.6.5 of Buckland et al. (2001) for formulae to compare density estimates.
